       LINK N3 OPPOSITION LANDOWNERS’ LIMITED EXCEPTIONS TO THE
      ALTERNATIVE RECOMMENDATION IN THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

        Link N3 Opposition Landowners (Link N3 Opponents) files these Limited Exceptions

 (Exceptions) to the alternative recommendation of route selection offered in the Proposal for

 Decision (PFD). Pursuant to the Exceptions and Replies Memorandum, filed August 20, 2026,

 these Limited Exceptions are timely filed on or before September 2, 2026. Link N3 Opponents

 does not except to the primary recommendation in the Proposal for Decision.

                                     I.   INTRODUCTION

        On March 26, 2026, Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (Oncor) and LCRA

 Transmission Services Corporation (LCRA) (collectively, Applicants) filed a joint application

 (Application) with the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission) to amend their

 certificates of convenience and necessity (CCNs) to construct, own, and operate a proposed Bell

 County East-to-Big Hill 765-kilovolt (kV) transmission line (Bell County East-to-Big Hill

 Project) in Bell, Burnet, Concho, Coryell, Lampasas, Llano, Mason, Mills, San Saba, Schleicher,
                                                                                                    Page 3 of 18


Tom Green, and Williamson counties, Texas.1 Link N3 Opponents does raise these exceptions

limited only to the PFD’s routing recommendation of Route 894 that would only be relevant if

the Commission rejects the primary recommendation of denial on the basis of need in the PFD.

The PFD does not provide a robust or persuasive analysis to recommend Route 894. In fact,

many of the unfavorable attributes and concerns associated with Route 894 are laid out in the

PFD and actually support selection of a route other than Route 894. The PFD’s routing analysis

does not address relevant Commission precedent that supports rejection of Route 894, in

particular where it affects the Lampasas River Valley and where it would cross the Colorado

River in proximity to the Colorado Bend State Park and the recently acquired Post Oak Ridge

State Park. Additionally, the PFD fails to give consideration to the landowners and attributes

contained in the Western half of the Study Area and focuses on the Eastern half although as

noted in the Application the proposed transmission line is vast approximately spanning 214 to

244 miles.2 Accordingly, if the Commission overturns the primary recommendation in the PFD

on need, Link N3 Opponents urges the Commission to review all of the routing options available

using a robust analysis of record evidence and Commission precedent and considering the

entirety of the impacts of any routing choice. Such an analysis will reflect that Routes 2963 or

Route 296 Option A4 better address the routing factors when considering the overall public

interest as required by the applicable law.

                                 II.      EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

   Link N3 Opponents files exceptions only on the basis of the PFD’s routing

    recommendation. The PFD provided limited analysis for its routing recommendation of

    Route 894 that failed to consider the overall public interest and the applicable routing

    factors as a whole.

   Route 296 performs better overall when considering all the routing factors and

    considering the mitigation opportunities available for Florence Elementary School.

   The PFD failed to consider these mitigation opportunities in addressing community

    values in the PFD.5

   Although the PFD addressed the severe bifurcation effects of using Route 894 on

    landowners, it still chose to recommend selection of the route.6

   Route 296 also performs better in paralleling compatible ROW overall.7

   Route 296 and Route 296 Option A also avoid the problematic Colorado River Crossings

    at Link J22 that is part of Route 894.8

   Route 296 and Route 296 Option A, unlike Route 894 does not come within the viewshed

    of Colorado Bend State Park or Post Oak Ridge State Park.9

   Route 296 and Route 296 Option A allows Rancho Bonito Livestock Company to

    continue using its helicopter operations for law enforcement and emergency services

    purposes.10

                                        III.     APPLICABLE LAW

        The Commission may only grant an amendment to a certificate of convenience and

necessity if it finds that the transmission facility is necessary for the service, accommodation,

convenience, or safety of the public.12 In reaching the decision on whether to grant the

amendment, the Commission must consider both the statutory factors found in PURA §

37.056(c) and the Commission’s rules found in 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B). In the PFD, the ALJs

correctly found that the Applicants failed to establish need under PURA § 37.056(a) and that the

application should be denied.

        If the Commission rejects the PFD’s recommendation on need, it should also overturn the

alternative routing recommendation in the PFD. The ALJs recommend the selection of the

Applicants’ “best meets” Route 894; however, this route does not represent a proper

consideration of the statutory factors or commission precedent, it ignores the well-developed

record that this route is contrary to community values, exhibits poor environmental metrics, and

treats a select few structures as constraints that through minor modifications could be avoided.

No single routing factor is dispositive, and the Commission is directed to consider the routing

factors in a proportional manner.

        As noted by the PFD, the Texas Third Court of Appeals stated “[n]one of the statutory

factors is intended to be absolute in the sense that any one shall prevail in all possible

                                            IV.     EXCEPTIONS

        Link N3 Opponents respectfully submits these Exceptions which are limited to the PFD’s

routing recommendation of Route 894. This route would decimate the Colorado River at a

previously undisturbed crossing that, according to the Texas Parks and Wildlife, will have

seriously detrimental impact on the Colorado Bend State Park and the Post Oak Ridge State

Park. Further, contrary to the Commission policies favoring paralleling of existing infrastructure

corridors and property lines, this route would bisect the properties along Link N315 and ignores

the Commission rule in 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(iii) for

paralleling property lines and not “apparent property lines.” Link N3 Opponents will show

through these exceptions that Route 894 was chosen based on a limited analysis that focused

almost exclusively on avoiding Florence Elementary School and a counting of habitable

structures rather than a consideration of the routing factors as a whole. Additionally, these

exceptions will demonstrate when focusing on community values, parks and recreation,

environmental integrity, cost, paralleling, and engineering constraints along with prudent

avoidance Route 296 and Route 296 Option outperform Route 894 when considering the overall

public interest.

a.     Routing Criteria

        i.          Community Values

       The Environmental Assessment (EA) states that community values “requires

consideration of values and resources essential to a local community[,]”16 and is identified under

PURA § 37.056(c) as a criteria for the Commission to consider. The PFD addresses both the

Florence Elementary School and Impacts to Landowners as part of Community Values.17

       N3 adopts the arguments made by Save the Lampasas 25, Inc. (Save the Lampasas) in its

exceptions regarding Florence Elementary School.18

       Regarding Impacts to Landowners, the PFD acknowledges that Route 894 bisects many

ranches on the eastern half of the Study Area but still selects Route 894 as its routing

recommendation.19 The N3 Group believes the analysis to impacts on landowners are not fully

weighed by the PFD. The PFD fails to acknowledge any of the bisection that occurs in the

western half of the Study Area. The use of Route 894 and Link N3 would bisect or fragment the

ranches of Angell Land and Livestock, LLC; Rancho Bonito Livestock Company; JHET Ranch,

LLC and the property of Kaddo Kothmann.20 Despite this and all the evidence laid out in the

PFD, the routing recommendation still recommended Route 894 by considering the paralleling of

“apparent” property boundaries and stating that Route 894 performed favorably on paralleling

existing compatible ROW.21

       The PFD also fails to make any mention of public engagement including public meeting

comments, protests, or interventions. Fragmentation or bisecting of property was a concern

       Both Routes 296 and Route 296 Option A avoid these problematic river crossings as

discussed below, and both options avoid placing a transmission line within 500 feet of Florence

Elementary School.30 However, rather than using a subjective balancing of factors as required

under the statute and the Commission’s rules, it is clear that the PFD gave little credence to the

routing factors overall and focused its analysis on the avoidance of Florence Elementary School.

Another flaw of the PFD was that it summarily excluded routes from the beginning for

“receiv[ing] considerably less discussion than the Focus Routes [894, 487, 392, and 296] during

hearing and briefing.”31 Less discussion of a route is not necessarily indicative of a reason not to

choose that route, in fact, discussion and attention in the can indicate as much a measure of

opposition to a route.

       As noted by Chairman Smitherman, “[t]he ultimate goal is to find a resolution that is least

harmful on the community and property owners while still complying with the statute and

applicable rules....”32 The routes that best accomplish this goal are Route 296 and Route 296

Option A.

        i.          Aesthetic and Historic Values

       Historical Values

       High Archeological sensitivity and the presence of cultural resources exist throughout the

Study Area and the N3 Opposition Landowners except to the PFD’s analysis of historical values

on the basis of simply counting the number of cultural resources recorded within 1,000 feet of

the route centerline.33 The PFD notes that “[t]here are 100 known historical or archeological sites

within 1,000 feet of feet of the centerline of one or more of the alternative routes.”34 The PFD

then goes on to describe that the Texas Historical Commission assigned Trinomial 41BT562 to

the Taylor-Rose Ranch located on Link G6 on Route 296.35 However, the entire property was not

marked until March 2026 the same month the instant CCN application was filed.36 Additionally,

the EA notes that “the overall site density and diversity indicate high archeological sensitivity

within the project area and support the likelihood of encountering additional unrecorded cultural

resources during future investigations.”37 The PFD itself even acknowledges that all proposed

routes that all routes cross through Burnet County where there are designated Heritage Ranches

with their historic significance acknowledged by the Texas Department of Agriculture, the Texas

Historical Commission, and the Burnet County Historical Commission. Additionally, Burnet

County was home to Comanche, Apache, and many other Native American tribes.38 The EA also

notes that the presence of National Register of Historical Places properties and districts and State

Antiquities Landmarks across multiple counties within the study area suggests that there is a high

Route 296 and 296 Option A perform equally well in this category and give credence to the

       Aesthetic Values

       The PFD addresses aesthetic values through a numerical counting of highway and street

crossings by different routes and by the estimated length of the route within the visual

foreground of highways.40 The PFD does away with the importance of aesthetic values to

landowners by simply stating that “[a] multitude of landowners expressed appreciation for the

aesthetic value of their property, regardless of which route would affect it.”41 There is more to

aesthetic values for landowners than is noted by the statement above.            As noted in the

Community Values section, the properties belong to Link N3 Opponents is comprised of rural

homesteads and working ranches and home to mostly native pastureland.42 These native

pasturelands “have motts of oaks, elms, and cedar trees that leave space for vistas that would be

altered by the clearing of trees and construction of a highly visible transmission line.”43 They

would also be altered by the bifurcation and fragmentation of the properties discussed in the

community values section. These impacts are also concerning for landowners since Route 894

would also come within 300 feet of two habitable structures belonging to the Link N3

Route 894 would have on aesthetics impacts to landowners, many of whom live and work on

their ranches. Route 296 and Route 296 Option A would avoid the bifurcation and destruction of

vistas for many in the Study Area and as noted in the Community Values section, more

intervenors are located on links N4 and N12 than N3.

         Environmental Integrity

        Link N3 Opponents adopts the argument on environmental integrity from Save the

Lampasas’s Exceptions.45 Additionally, while the PFD focuses on the eastern portion of the

Study Area, on the western portion, JHET Ranch, located on Link N3, is a thriving sanctuary for

flora and fauna and over the years the owners have confirmed many sightings of migratory birds

and wildlife.46 The JCS Ranch and Angell Land and Livestock Ranch are home to several, large,

old live oak trees and white-tail and axis deer, turkey, dove, and quail and the building of Link

N3 could disrupt the use of the land by wildlife and livestock on the ranch.47 The Kothmanns use

their property for ranching and hunting and raise cattle and goat on the property.48 It is important

to focus on impacts to the Study Area as a whole and not simply those environmental integrity

impacts located on the eastern half of the Study Area. It is clear throughout the PFD that little

focus has been given to the western half of the Study Area, even though the length of the

transmission line spans 223.17 miles if Route 894 is chosen. Overall, each half of the Study Area

has remarkably different ecological, environmental, and landowner concerns and the entire Study

Area should be given its due consideration for the routing factors.

Royal Netherlands Air Force 302 Squadron uses the property for training exercises and describes

access to the ranch as providing “essential training opportunities.”55 In addition, the helicopter

was registered with AirMed and can be used for medical emergencies.56 It has been used to assist

farms that consist of more than one tax parcel, resulting in a higher total compatible ROW

        Proposing and endorsing routes with low paralleling attributes lead to more intrusions

and fragmentation of historic, multigenerational property, and to the burdening of the property

by the applicant’s construction and maintenance activities.65 As a result, the Commission should

not approve Route 894 which is an abject departure from any routing criteria and a departure

from any of the concerns regarding paralleling noted in the PFD. Route 296 or Route 296 Option

A should be chosen as it clearly performs better regarding this routing criteria.

       iv.          Prudent Avoidance

        Although prudent avoidance was pointed to by the ALJs as a reason that they

recommended Route 894 over Route 296, Route 296 in fact compares favorably to Route 894

when the issue is analyzed comprehensively in the way its definition demands.                   As

acknowledged in the PFD,66 the Commission defines prudent avoidance as “[t]he limiting of

exposures to electric and magnetic fields that can be avoided with reasonable investments of

money and effort.”67 The ALJs further acknowledged that “[p]rudent avoidance does not mean

that a proposed transmission line must avoid habitable structures at all costs, but that reasonable

alternatives must be considered.”68 However, after immediately acknowledging this, the PFD

appears to then cabin its general analysis of prudent avoidance strictly to the amount of habitable

structures on each route.69 When giving its routing recommendation, the PFD then explicitly

states that “Route 894 performs favorably on habitable structures,”70 rather than using the term

“prudent avoidance.” In the three sentences it uses to explain its process on prudent avoidance,

the PFD appears to conflate “habitable structures” and “prudent avoidance” as like-for-like,

when Commission rules and precedent require a much more comprehensive approach.

       Any of Route 296’s negative externalities, specifically regarding its proximity to the

Florence Elementary School and two churches, can be easily mitigated by choosing either Route

296 or Route 296 Option A.

       Link N3 Opponents urges that a simple count of habitable structures does not constitute a

        The Commission may only grant an amendment to a certificate of convenience and

necessity if it finds that the transmission facility is necessary for the service, accommodation,

convenience, or safety of the public.12 In reaching the decision on whether to grant the

amendment, the Commission must consider both the statutory factors found in PURA §

37.056(c) and the Commission's rules found in 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B). In the PFD, the ALJs

correctly found that the Applicants failed to establish need under PURA § 37.056(a) and that the

application should be denied.

        If the Commission rejects the PFD's recommendation on need, it should also overturn the

alternative routing recommendation in the PFD.                 The ALJs recommend the selection of the

Applicants' "best meets" Route 894; however, this route does not represent a proper

consideration of the statutory factors or commission precedent, it ignores the well-developed

record that this route is contrary to community values, exhibits poor environmental metrics, and

treats a select few structures as constraints that through minor modifications could be avoided.

No single routing factor is dispositive, and the Commission is directed to consider the routing

factors in a proportional manner.
